title: Randomness Requirements for Security
subtitle: Why a secret key is only as strong as the dice that rolled it.
summary: RFC 4086 explains how to produce random numbers that an attacker cannot guess, which every password, key and nonce depends on. Its central warning is that numbers can look random and pass statistical tests yet still be predictable, because they came from a small space such as a clock value. It surveys physical entropy sources, ways to clean and combine them, and cryptographically strong generators that stretch a small seed into many bits. It replaced RFC 1750 and is Best Current Practice 106.

eli5.summary: If you pick a secret by rolling a die, nobody can guess it, but if you always pick it by looking at the clock, a sneaky friend can try every time of day. This document teaches computers to roll real dice.

questions: why is a clock a bad random seed
what is the difference between dev random and dev urandom
how many bits of randomness does a password need
what is a pseudo random number generator
how do you de-skew a random bit stream

tldr.problem: Security depends on secrets that attackers cannot guess, but ordinary pseudo-random generators and clocks give far fewer unpredictable bits than they appear to.
tldr.mechanism: Gather entropy from physical or hard-to-observe sources, de-skew and mix it with a strong hash or cipher into a seed, then stretch the seed with a cryptographically strong generator.
tldr.outcome: A few hundred truly unpredictable bits are enough for even very high security, and the pitfalls it lists still cause real key-generation failures.

today: The ideas in RFC 4086 are now built into operating systems. Linux, the BSDs and macOS expose a kernel generator through /dev/urandom or a system call, and Windows provides CryptGenRandom and its successors, so most programmers never gather entropy by hand. Hardware random-number instructions on modern CPUs follow the document's advice to include a physical source. The standards it cites as work in progress, such as ANSI X9.82, were later superseded by NIST publications, and the specific algorithms it describes (DES-based generators, SHA-1, MD5) are dated, though the reasoning about entropy, mixing and seeding still holds.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Systems such as SSH, IPsec, TLS, S/MIME, PGP, DNSSEC and Kerberos use strong cryptography to protect against snooping and spoofing. The RFC points out a flaw at their heart: all of them need secret, unguessable numbers, and the lack of generally available sources of truly unpredictable numbers is, in the authors' words, "an open wound in the design of cryptographic software."

The requirement is not that numbers look random. It is that an adversary has a very low probability of guessing or determining them. That fails easily when a generator passes traditional statistical tests, or draws on a limited-range source such as a clock, because the attacker may only have to search "an embarrassingly small space of possibilities."

RFC 4086 is a Best Current Practice that replaces RFC 1750 from 1994. It recommends that future systems include hardware random-number generation, suggests fallbacks when none exists, and works through how many random bits sample applications need.
sections.eli5: Locks only help if nobody can guess the key. Computers make keys by picking numbers, and if they pick them badly, a burglar can guess them in a few tries.

sections.title: What Random Means for Security
sections.content:
Two kinds of random quantity are wanted. A human-usable password only has to be unguessable, even if every byte has its top bit zero. A fixed-length key should also look truly random, so that its bits pass statistical tests. Both must resist guessing by trial and error.

The RFC measures this with information theory. If there are 2^n equally likely values, n bits of information are present and an attacker must try about 2^(n-1) on average. A 128-bit key from a generator with an 8-bit seed holds only 8 bits of information, since the attacker just runs the generator on all 256 seeds.

Shannon entropy can mislead. A generator that outputs zero half the time and otherwise a random 128-bit value has 64 bits of Shannon entropy, yet an attacker who guesses zero breaks half of all uses. So the RFC recommends min-entropy, defined as minus the log (base 2) of the largest single probability, which is 1 bit in that example. It is the most conservative member of the Renyi entropy family.

Statistical randomness is not unpredictability. Using AES with a constant key to encrypt 1, 2, 3 and so on gives output with excellent statistics that anyone can predict, while die rolls written as ASCII are statistically poor but unpredictable.
sections.eli5: A shuffled-looking list is no good if the other kids know how it was shuffled. What counts is whether anyone can guess it, not whether it looks messy.

sections.title: Entropy Sources
sections.content:
An entropy source supplies the real unpredictability that everything else builds on. The RFC says less is needed than people think: even the highest-security systems are unlikely to need strong keying material of much over 200 bits, and a few hundred random bits at start-up or once a day, stretched by a strong generator, is enough.

Sound and video input
A microphone jack with nothing plugged in, or a camera with the lens cap on, yields essentially thermal noise. It needs de-skewing and a check for hardware failure.
Disk drives
Air turbulence causes tiny fluctuations in rotation speed that show up in seek timing. The data is highly correlated and needs strong processing.
Ring oscillators
Odd-length loops of gates sampled at a fixed rate, XORed together; IEEE 802.11i suggests rings of 19, 23 and 29 gates.
External events
Keystroke and mouse timing, or network arrival times, are usable but can be repetitive or manipulated by an adversary.

Clocks and serial numbers are weak. A clock may deliver far fewer changing bits than its nominal resolution, and a hardware address such as an Ethernet MAC address is structured and often guessable from its manufacturer or date. On small, single-user or embedded systems, especially at start-up, an attacker may rebuild the same inputs, so a hardware source is preferable.
sections.eli5: Real surprise comes from messy things in the world, like static on a radio or the exact moment you press a key. A clock is not a surprise, because everyone can see it.

sections.title: De-skewing and Mixing
sections.content:
Raw entropy is rarely uniform, but the RFC notes the distribution need not be. All that is needed is a conservative estimate of how non-uniform it is. De-skewing removes bias. Taking the parity of a long run of bits works for any skew: even if a source gives 99% ones, the parity of 308 samples is within 0.001 of 50/50. Von Neumann's method reads non-overlapping pairs, drops 00 and 11, and maps 01 to 0 and 10 to 1. Reading overlapping pairs by mistake would produce a perfectly predictable alternating sequence.

Mixing combines several imperfect inputs so that the output keeps the entropy of the best one. A strong mixing function makes every output bit a complex non-linear function of all input bits, so a change to one input bit flips about half the output bits. AES and hash functions such as SHA-1 are named as good mixers. Hashing those 308 skewed bits with SHA-1 retains the over 5 bits of information they contain, instead of the single bit that parity gives.

Mixing cannot create entropy. Four 32-bit inputs with 12 bits of unpredictability each give at most 48 bits out, however long the output is. Diffie-Hellman is not recommended as a mixing function.
sections.eli5: If a coin lands heads too often, you can flip it twice and keep only the pairs that differ. Mixing is like stirring paint from several cans so the odd color of one can does not matter.

sections.title: Pseudo-random Number Generators
sections.content:
Once a seed holds enough entropy, an algorithm can stretch it into as many bits as needed. These generators are platform independent, but their internals and state must stay hidden from the adversary, and the RFC warns that designing one "is not a task for amateurs."

Section 6.1 lists bad ideas. Complex manipulation does not help if the seed is small, such as a clock value, and blindly chosen complexity can even destroy the entropy of a good seed; Knuth's example algorithm quickly collapsed into a repeated value or a small cycle. Selecting from a large public database buys only the entropy of the starting point, perhaps "a little over a couple of dozen bits" for 32 bytes taken from Usenet. Linear congruential and shift-register generators are predictable from short observed output, and polynomial congruential generators can all be broken.

The good approach is a strong seed, cryptographically strong steps, and not revealing the full generator state in the output. Examples are hashing the seed with successive counters, counter (CTR) and output feedback (OFB) encryption, and Blum Blum Shub, whose prediction is provably as hard as factoring n when you use only the lowest-order bit or at most log2(log2(s)) low bits. Many systems keep an entropy pool: mix new bits in, extract bits out, and save the state at shutdown.
sections.eli5: A good magic trick starts from one real surprise and then makes a long show out of it. A bad one just repeats a pattern a clever watcher can learn.

sections.title: Generators in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC describes standards and deployed systems in two groups. The first group includes its own entropy source. The US Department of Defense password recommendation uses DES in 64-bit output feedback mode with an initialization vector from the clock and IDs, a key from interrupt, status and counter registers, and 64 bits typed by an administrator as plaintext.

The Linux random device keeps a pool of 512 bytes, as 128 words of 4 bytes. Keyboard, disk and mouse events are XORed in and stirred with a degree-128 primitive polynomial. Output is the SHA-1 hash of the pool, 20 bytes at a time. /dev/random blocks when the entropy estimate reaches zero and suits long-term keys; /dev/urandom does not block, which may be adequate for session keys. Windows CryptGenRandom feeds a stored seed and system data to SHA-1 and uses the result to seed an RC4 key stream.

The second group assumes a good seed is supplied. These are the ANSI X9.82 HMAC-based generator, X9.17 key generation with DES, and the NIST DSS generator. The HMAC generator is short enough to sketch below.
sections.eli5: Real computers already have a bucket of surprises that they stir all day. Programs just ask the bucket for as many random numbers as they need.

sections.title: How Much Randomness Is Enough
sections.content:
Section 8 works two examples. For passwords, assume an attacker can try one guess every six seconds, which is about 5,000,000 tries a year, and monthly log checks make 500,000 tries the realistic worst case. A one-in-a-thousand chance of success then needs at least 500,000,000 passwords, about 2^29, so 29 bits of randomness. That is a three-word phrase from a 1,000-word list, or six case-insensitive letters and digits. Each extra factor of 1,000 adds about 10 bits: 39 bits for one in a million and 49 bits for one in a billion.

For a very high security symmetric key, the RFC assumes an attacker checks 10^10 keys per second, about 2.4*10^15 per month, which needs at least 63 bits just to survive a month. The 1996 key-length study the RFC cites recommends 75 to 90 bits for 1995, and adding 2/3 of a bit per year puts a reasonable range at 81 to 96 bits for 2004. A meet-in-the-middle attack on a composite cipher can halve the exponent, which doubles the requirement to 192 bits.

The RFC itself calls such key-length calculations "controversial," because they depend on assumptions about the algorithm. They show the order of magnitude, not exact rules.
sections.eli5: The longer and more surprising your secret, the more guesses a thief needs. A short secret falls fast, and a long, truly random one would take longer than anyone can wait.

sections.title: Conclusion and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The conclusion is that generating unguessable secret quantities is "an essential but difficult task." The hardware needed to do it is simple, and the volume is small, so audio input or disk drives already present in most machines can do the job. Cheap computational techniques can then turn weak inputs from several sources into a smaller amount of higher-quality keying material. From a few hundred bits of good seed, cryptographically strong sequences supply everything else.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: the whole document concerns generating unguessable "random" quantities for passwords, cryptographic keys, initialization vectors, sequence numbers and similar uses. A failure here undermines every algorithm built on top, no matter how strong. Elsewhere the RFC notes a TCP use: random initial sequence numbers, as discussed in RFC 1948, are one more place randomness is needed.
sections.eli5: Everything secret on a computer depends on a good first roll of the dice. Roll it badly and the strongest lock in the world is easy to open.

items.title: Physical
items.text: Thermal noise, radioactive decay, ring oscillators and noisy diodes sampled by a fast clock.

items.title: Existing hardware
items.text: Sound or video input with nothing connected, and disk seek timing.

items.title: User and system events
items.text: Keystroke and mouse timing, interrupts and packet arrivals, trusted only if an adversary cannot manipulate them.

items.title: Weak on their own
items.text: System clocks and hardware serial numbers give fewer real bits than they appear to.

data.title: HMAC-based generator, simplified
data.code:
# Initialize
V = 0x01 0x01 ... 0x01          # every byte 00000001, hash_length bytes
K = 0x00 0x00 ... 0x00          # hash_length bytes
K = HMAC(K, V | 0x00 | input_entropy)
V = HMAC(K, V)
K = HMAC(K, V | 0x01 | input_entropy)
V = HMAC(K, V)

# Generate (temp starts empty)
V = HMAC(K, V)
temp = temp | V                 # repeat until enough bits
# return the leading bits of temp, then update:
K = HMAC(K, V | 0x00)
V = HMAC(K, V)
